items.question: How did your view of computational approaches to understanding the mind change during your PhD?
items.object: Computational approaches to understanding the mind
items.answer: When I was choosing a program to do my PhD in, I was actually trying to get away to some extent from computer science. I was looking for something different, and I ended up focusing more on experimental human psycholinguistics for my PhD, at least at first. I was doing a lot of cognitive neuroscience, actually, with this exotic machine called MEG, and that's what I was doing for the first few years of my PhD. But then gradually, as time went on, I realized that the computational approaches to understanding the mind were the ones that I find maybe more promising than the kind of purely experimental ones. The thesis ended up being a combination of computational and experimental work. None of it was AI per se; it was more like using machine learning to understand what humans do in experiments.

The thesis ended up being a combination of computational and experimental work. None of it was AI per se; it was more like using machine learning to understand what humans do in experiments.

items.question: How do you think language models should be evaluated to determine whether they understand linguistic structure?
items.object: Evaluating language models’ understanding of linguistic structure
items.answer: I think evaluation has gotten a lot more sophisticated in the last decade. When I was just getting into the field, the way you would evaluate a language model, let's say a system designed to predict the next word, was by having it predict the next word in a new text that it wasn't trained on and seeing how successful it was: how high was the probability that it assigned to the words that occurred in that text? But the issue with that form of evaluation is that it's pretty easy to predict the next word without knowing a lot about the structure of the sentence. In most sentences, you can do pretty well just by looking at the most recent three or four words. If you're able to memorize sequences of words, you can do pretty well at predicting the next word. So to really determine if you have a certain linguistic ability or reasoning ability, you need to construct specific sentences, or find specific sentences in your corpus, where it's really important to understand the structure of the sentence to be able to predict the next word. You want to ignore all the cases where you can predict the next word with these cheaper tricks, let's say, and focus on cases where the only way the model is able to predict the next word correctly is if it figured out the structure of the argument or the sentence. That's the kind of thing that we do in psychology as well when we work with humans. We try to create materials that are matched for everything else except the one thing that we are trying to compare between two different groups, or the one thing that we're trying to evaluate in this person's ability.

items.question: How do you assess behavioral similarity between language models and humans as evidence that they use similar internal representations?
items.object: Behavioral similarity as evidence that language models and humans use similar internal representations
items.answer: First of all, I would be skeptical of the argument that two systems behave exactly the same way. But basically, what was being said is, if two systems behave in exactly the same way, then that's a really good starting point for assuming that the model works in the same way as a human. In fact, there's very little that we know about humans' internal representations that is not derived from human behavior. It's not like we have any direct access to humans' internal representations. What we know from neuroscience is very basic. Our techniques don't really allow us to reconstruct the representations in the same detail that studying human behavior and the kinds of mistakes you make, for example, can teach us. So I would say that behavioral analysis is basically most of what we have to go on. It's very likely, I guess, that if the system makes exactly the same errors that a human makes, there's something similar about the representations that the system and the human use. At least that's most of what we have to go on. The one caveat is that we should probably also try to match the development of the system and the human. It's much more likely that their representations will be the same if the systems are exposed to the same training data that a human might be exposed to. That's a big difference we have these days between commercially available language models and humans: we train our language models in a grammatically different way from humans. It's likely that, because of that, the representations that evolve are different from the ones that humans evolve. My hunch, though, is that if their representations are really different, there's going to be a behavioral effect of that difference. They're going to make different errors than humans, and in fact that is what we're seeing in the behavioral evidence. I think you're asking a very good question about whether there could be two systems with exactly the same behavior but different representations. The answer is probably yes, but it's almost unknowable, given how little we know about humans' internal representations that isn't derived from their behavior.

items.question: How do you interpret language models’ superhuman memory abilities as evidence about whether their internal representations resemble humans’ representations?
items.object: Language models’ superhuman memory and their similarity to humans
items.answer: I guess there's one thing that may not be clear from what I said before: it's not that our models are so good that they're becoming closer and closer to humans and therefore we can't conclude that there are differences in their representations. In fact, what's happening in a lot of cases is the opposite direction: the models are becoming less and less like humans, which I think leads to the conclusion that their internal representations are different from humans. Let me give you a couple of examples. The language models that we have right now have much greater working memory capacity than humans. You can give a language model a list of 200 words and ask it to repeat that list, and it will repeat it verbatim without any problems. This is not something any human can do. The models are able to memorize very long sequences from the training data. This is all from work that I've been involved in. You can see that a model is able to repeat very long speeches that have occurred in its training data a few times. Those are superhuman abilities in some sense. They're maybe not that impressive, because it's easy to write a computer program that gives you back a list of 200 words that you give to it, but they show very clearly that the representations the models are using are different from the representations that humans are using. It's not necessarily a bad thing. I think it's good for computers to be better than humans, and you don't want a calculator to make the same mistakes as a human when multiplying really big numbers. But it does show that the calculator has very different representations from humans.

items.question: How do you understand the role of hierarchical sentence structure in explaining subject-verb agreement?
items.object: Hierarchical syntactic structure in subject-verb agreement
items.answer: This is a well-known fact in linguistics: you can't always model sentences as just sequences of words. In most cases, the correct way to represent a sentence is as a structured entity that has groupings of words, each called constituents, organized in a hierarchical way. You have a big constituent that is constituted by two smaller constituents. It's not just a sequence of words. Let me give you an example, using the specific example from the paper: subject-verb agreement. In English, if you have a present tense verb in the third person, it has to agree in number with the subject. If the subject is singular, the verb also needs to be singular, like “the dog runs.” If the subject is plural, the verb also needs to be plural, like “the dogs run.” You might think it's easy to learn because the dog is right next to the word “runs,” so you can just memorize sequences of words: dog goes with runs and dogs goes with run. But it doesn't always work that way, because sometimes you'll have a noun right next to the verb that's actually not the relevant noun. It would be something like “the dogs in the park run.” “Park” is a singular word, but that's not the subject; it's irrelevant. You're supposed to ignore it and know that the subject is the word “dogs” that occurred a lot earlier. Sometimes you have many nouns in the sentence, and to figure out which of those nouns determines whether the verb should be singular or plural, you need to understand the structure of the sentence. The structure isn't written in the sentence; it's latent, something you need to infer from the sequence of words. That's the premise of the field of syntax in linguistics: there's a lot of structure behind each sentence that's not literally represented in the sequence of words.

You have a big constituent that is constituted by two smaller constituents. It's not just a sequence of words.

items.question: How do you look back on your choice of subject-verb agreement as an early test of LSTM language models?
items.object: Subject-verb agreement as an early test of LSTM language models
items.answer: The reason we started with subject-verb agreement is that it's so simple. I mean, I was able to describe it in 30 seconds, and many, many sentences have that dependency. In retrospect, 10 years later, it looks like we were kind of lowballing it. It was an easy thing for the model to do, but we were actually quite surprised that the models were able to do that at all at the time. It goes to show how different our expectations have become from deep learning models. At the time, LSTM language models were just coming on the scene, and no one knew what they were able to do. That's why we started with such a simple, pervasive phenomenon.

items.question: How do you think about what makes some linguistic phenomena harder than others for language models to learn?
items.object: Differences in difficulty among linguistic phenomena for language models
items.answer: There are a lot of phenomena that are a lot less frequent in the training data. Then it becomes a question of how many examples of this phenomenon you need to learn it, and whether we're able to learn from the same number of examples that a human is able to learn these things. There are definitely easier and harder phenomena, not just because of their frequency, but that's one big issue. Since we worked on that paper, many other phenomena, from people in my group and a bunch of other groups, have been tested in language models in many different languages, and the picture is mixed. In some cases, the results were less impressive than in the cases we looked at in the first study.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between a neural network's ability to reverse a list and the symbolic structure of its internal representations?
items.object: Implicit symbolic structure in neural network representations
items.answer: This ties in with something that came up earlier in our conversation: if a system behaves in a certain way, then you sometimes need to conclude from that behavior that it has a certain kind of representation. In a neural network, the representations are always vectors; they're distributed representations. Instead of the way you would think about a list—let's say you had a list of numbers and were asked to reverse it, and the list was 1, 6, 4—the symbolic way to reverse it would be to say, “The thing that was in the last position was four; let me produce that first. Then the thing in the second-to-last position was six, so let me produce that,” and so on. That is a symbolic algorithm because it uses categories like first position, second position, four, and six. Those are symbols. In a neural network, the representations are all vectors. You have one vector that represents the sequence 164 and then maybe another vector that represents the reverse of it, 461. If you're a neural network designed to reverse a list, you're supposed to take that vector as an input and produce the other vector as an output. What we argue is that, to the extent the neural network is able to reverse the sequence, it must at least implicitly have representations that reflect the symbolic structure of the list. It's not literally running Python code that has symbols in it, but there's an isomorphism of sorts between the vectors the system uses to represent the lists and the symbolic structure that we hypothesize is required to perform this task. In that paper, mostly Tom McCoy, who was a lead author, proposed a method for mapping a hypothesis about the symbolic structure we think is represented in the vectors onto a set of vectors we get from a neural network. We found a very remarkable correspondence between our hypothesis and the system's internal representation. This shows that if the network has a lot of evidence that it needs to perform a symbolic task, like taking a string of symbols and reversing it, then it is capable of developing internal representations that are basically isomorphic to the symbolic representations we think are necessary to do this task. By isomorphic, I just mean there is some mapping between the structure of the vector representations and the symbolic theory that we have in mind.

items.question: How do you understand the difference between learning symbolic structure in a task like list reversal and learning it from natural language?
items.object: Learning symbolic structure in list reversal versus natural language
items.answer: The very simple tasks we looked at in that paper, like reversing a list, are tasks where it's clear that the only way to solve them is by having some sort of symbolic representation of which number was in which place in that list. You give the model a lot of evidence in inputs and output pairs that it can only map if it figured out that there's some sort of symbolic structure there. When it comes to natural language, it gets messier because, as I mentioned before, in many cases you can get away with cheaper tricks. You can fake it; it can give the impression that you understand something about the sentence without really knowing which word occurred first and which word occurred afterwards. We have a lot of work showing that the models do, in fact, learn those tricks instead of the structured representation that will generalize in all cases. You'll do well on 95% of the cases, but then there'll be the 5% where things go wrong.

items.question: Why do you see value in more complex architectures such as tree-structured neural networks for learning structured representations?
items.object: Inductive bias in tree-structured neural networks and other structured architectures
items.answer: What this shows is that for some of the simpler architectures, they need a lot of evidence that the domain is structured to learn those structured representations. If you don't give them a ton of evidence, they will get lazy and do something simpler. If you have an architecture like the tree-structured neural network, or other architectures that are less lazy in that sense, you can learn from a smaller amount of evidence that the representations need to be structured. That's called an inductive bias: the learner has some sort of tendency to develop the right representations that lead it to generalize in the way that you wanted to. That's where I think the motivation for the more complex architectures comes in. They require less evidence to learn and generalize in the appropriate structural way.

items.question: Why do you consider it problematic to evaluate language models trained on different amounts of data head to head on the same dataset?
items.object: Pretraining-agnostic evaluation of language models
items.answer: What I call pretraining agnostic is that you take two different models that are trained on different datasets, but you evaluate them head to head on the same dataset. That is problematic. The reason it's problematic is that you're not giving the more data-efficient model a chance to succeed, because the model trained on more data may succeed using certain tricks, certain memorization techniques, that the model trained on less data can't resort to. Just to give a sense of the discrepancy between the amounts of data the models are trained on, it's gotten a lot worse since I wrote that paper a few years ago. Our estimates of how many words a human hears before college in the United States would be something like 50 million to 100 million. The big language models we train these days, like PaLM, ChatGPT, and so on, are trained on trillions of words. Those are many orders of magnitude more words. If you compare a human or a model trained on a small amount of data to models trained on a lot of data, the models trained on a lot of data can solve tasks by copying examples from the training set, or finding examples in the training set very similar to the example they're asked to do something with. Humans and models trained on less data are forced to use a more sophisticated generalization technique, just because it's different enough from anything they've seen before. We've worked a lot on compositionality, where you have a complex sentence made up of two simpler sentences, but they're combined in a way that's unfamiliar to you. If you're human or a model trained on 50 million words, the only way you could understand that more complex sentence is by taking simpler sentences that might be similar to what we've seen before and combining them using an algorithm of combining meanings. But a model trained on two trillion words has very likely seen that structure before. It's not going to be new to the model; it's not going to have to generalize, just use some sort of memorization-related trick. That's why it doesn't really make sense to evaluate the two kinds of models in the same way.

items.question: How do you assess the shift from large-scale task-specific fine-tuning to few-shot learning in light of your critique of identically distributed evaluation?
items.object: Identically distributed evaluation and the shift to few-shot learning
items.answer: If you teach the model a task by giving it a lot of examples—say, you give it two sentences and ask whether the second sentence follows from the first one, meaning that every time the first one is true, the second one also has to be true—that's a common evaluation task. You give the model 100,000 examples of the task and then ask it to perform the task on another set of a thousand examples. Usually, when that happens, the model can learn to perform the task in a way that doesn't reflect what you would want it to do. It will learn various properties of that dataset, and because the training and test sets have the same distribution, any pattern it finds in the training set is also going to apply to the test set. I think it's not that controversial that fine-tuning a model on 100,000 examples and then testing it on more examples from exactly the same distribution might lead to misleading results, where there might be some signal correlated with the labels in the training set that the model can then apply to the test set. That has changed quite a bit in the last few years. People don't evaluate models by fine-tuning them on hundreds of thousands of examples anymore, which I think is great. One surprising citation I remember reading in the GPT-3 paper was that they cited my position piece: “Look, now we're doing few-shot learning. We're just showing the model a couple of examples and it's generalizing from those two examples. We don't need to do fine-tuning anymore.” That addresses the issue I brought up in my position piece. I think it's questionable whether the models do in fact do zero-shot or few-shot learning, but if they do, that addresses the concerns I had in that paper. The other concern, the training-data-size issue, is only getting worse.

items.question: How do you see the relative promise of data-efficient learning and cross-lingual transfer for languages with less training data?
items.object: Data-efficient learning and cross-lingual transfer for low-resource languages
items.answer: When I said it's getting worse, I meant that the difference in training data between people and models is increasing. I'm not sure that's so bad for the applications that PaLM or whatever is designed for. The jury is still out. One thing that's clearly the case is that we don't have the same amount of data for English as for all other languages. We can find 10 trillion words in English on the internet, but we're not going to be able to find that for Maltese or a smaller language with fewer speakers. I think it's an open question how far we can get by training models on a huge amount of data from English and then using cross-lingual transfer techniques to import that knowledge into, let's say, a Maltese language model. It's possible that if we had models able to learn from less data, we would do better in low-resource languages, but another way to do better in low-resource languages is to improve cross-lingual transfer.

items.question: Why do you think learning from less data matters for language models used to study human cognition?
items.object: Human learning constraints in cognitive models of language
items.answer: There are two goals for having models that can learn from less data. One is the more applied goal: being able to learn in a domain where you have less data, or in a language where you have less data. That's a clear applied goal. The other goal is the cognitive modeling goal. Even if this doesn't directly advance AI, it's very likely we'll have better models of human language processing and the human brain if those models operate under the same constraints that humans do. There's a lot of work now that takes GPT-4 or GPT-3 and looks at its internal vectors and maps those vectors into brain activity. That's a really interesting direction, but I think we're going to get better at modeling brain activity if we have models that are more similar, that learn in the same way humans do and with the same constraints.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between word predictability and human reading difficulty in your study “Surprisal Does Not Explain Syntactic Disambiguation Difficulty”?
items.object: The relationship between word predictability and human processing difficulty in “Surprisal Does Not Explain Syntactic Disambiguation Difficulty”
items.answer: It's one of my favorite projects. We can only measure human processing difficulty indirectly. By processing difficulty, I mean something like this person takes longer to read this word, or maybe if we track their eye movements they get stuck on that word, reread it, or go back and reread it again. That's how processing difficulty is reflected in behavioral measurements from human experiments. In that study, we used a very simple technique called self-paced reading. We have the person read the sentence word by word. To move to the next word, the person has to press the space bar or some keys, and they only see one word at a time. You can see that when a word is surprising, people linger on it more than when it's less surprising. That's something we know across the board: predictable words are read faster than unpredictable words. That's not controversial. If you have a good computational model of word prediction, like the language models we have, you can take the predictability estimates from the language model and use them to predict human reading times. That gives you a sense of how similar the word predictions the models are making are to the word predictions humans are making. Then you can determine how much of the processing difficulty humans experience in different kinds of sentences has to do with word predictability versus other factors. Let me give you an example of one type of sentence that people in psycholinguistics have classically shown people experience a lot of processing difficulty with. Those are called garden path sentences. Sometimes when you say them out loud they don't sound as confusing as when you read them. It would be something like, “The student read the newspaper was going out of business.” Usually people start reading that sentence and think, “Okay, the student read the newspaper, great,” but then it turns out that's not what happened. The student read a story about the newspaper going out of business. You have one interpretation at the beginning of the sentence and then have to revise. That's the intuition behind that class of sentences. In that study, we looked at those particularly difficult sentences and asked to what extent the predictability estimates from the language model could explain the processing difficulty people experience. The conclusion was that they really do not explain that processing difficulty. One interpretation is that language models are just not very surprised by the words because, as with the working memory issue we discussed before, they are better than people at considering multiple interpretations of the sentence at the same time. They're not as surprised as we are. There's evidence that the better the language model is at predicting the next word, the worse it becomes at matching human reading. That supports the conclusion that language models are so much better at reading than we are as humans with our limited capacity. They don't have to make the same compromises that humans do, and they can just read faster, so to speak, though that analogy is very loose.

items.question: How do you think experience reading languages or genres with very complex sentences might shape your reading strategies?
items.object: Reading strategies developed through experience with complex sentences
items.answer: I've been spending a lot of time reading in German. It's one of my summer projects, and most German novels have extremely complex sentences like the ones you just mentioned, with a lot of what's called center embedding, where you have a sentence that kind of breaks up another sentence in the middle, then you go back to the earlier sentence and need to keep that in your memory. It's interesting, actually, that, as far as I know—if I remember correctly, I'm not an expert on this—German speakers are better at parsing center-embedded sentences than English speakers, just because they have so much more practice at it from those insanely convoluted sentence structures. That's a really interesting question. I don't know the answer to whether people reading novels with very complex sentences, or people used to reading in more complex genres or languages, have different reading strategies from the average person. That sounds very plausible to me. I definitely catch myself, reading in German, noticing that some verbs are famously split in half: you put one half at the end of the sentence and the other half at the beginning. I often catch myself, when I see the first half, knowing that something is going to happen all the way at the end of the sentence, so I go to the end of the sentence and read that, then come back. I'm not sure whether German speakers who have more practice than me do that as well, but I wouldn't be surprised. Anyway, I'm just speculating here. This isn't something I've done academic work on.

items.question: How do you see the role of model architecture in learning syntax, based on your paper “How to Plant Trees in Language Models”?
items.object: Transformer architecture and syntactic generalization in “How to Plant Trees in Language Models”
items.answer: The starting point is the discourse around scaling laws in the language modeling and deep learning world. What people usually do in that work is plot on the x-axis the number of FLOPs the model was trained on—basically, how much computation happened during training—or the number of parameters in the model, some very coarse-grained measure of how big it is. On the y-axis, you have the model's performance on some task. What we asked in that paper is whether it's really just about how much data you throw at the model or how big the model is, or whether there are properties of the architecture that affect how likely the model is to learn to generalize in the correct way, consistent with the linguistic structure of the sentence, and not with sequences of words that are correlated but don't capture the sentence's structure. With subject-verb agreement: are you going to learn to identify the subject, or use a strategy based on sequences of words that will work sometimes but fail in other cases? In that study, we didn't explore different architectures exactly. We stuck to the same architecture, the Transformer, which is what all the language models use these days, but looked at different shapes of the Transformer. You can have the same number of parameters but allocate them differently to the depth versus the width. You can have the embeddings be 200-dimensional versus 1,000-dimensional, multiplying the number of parameters by five, or multiply the number of layers by five; the total number of parameters can be the same, but the way they're allocated across the layers is different. We found some preliminary evidence, and we're currently following up in a more controlled study, suggesting that deeper models are more likely to learn the correct syntactic behavior than shallower models if you keep the number of parameters constant. It's better to have a deeper model than a wide model. That's the kind of experiment that is an antidote to taking the very bird's-eye view of just how big the model is. It does matter how you structure the model. My sense is that if you take a model quite different from a Transformer, like the models you mentioned before, you might get much stronger syntactic generalization from a much smaller amount of data or computation.

items.question: What do you make of your finding that a Transformer learns syntax faster from child-directed speech than from Wikipedia or internet data?
items.object: Child-directed speech as training data for learning syntax
items.answer: The other part of the paper looked at how fast the model learns to generalize correctly when trained on different types of language. Usually you train models on data from the internet, or in some experiments on something like Wikipedia. We were curious what would happen if you trained them instead on the language a child hears growing up. We used the child-directed speech corpus CHILDES, a collection of transcribed recordings from interactions between caregivers and children. We trained exactly the same Transformer model on different types of data. Surprisingly to me, it looks like when you train the model on child-directed speech, it actually learns syntax faster than when you train it on Wikipedia or internet data. The corpus has only about 10 million words, even less than a child would hear growing up, but even that seems to be enough to teach the Transformer a lot about syntax. That's what we meant by cognitively plausible. There might be something about the simpler language used when you communicate with a child that clues you into the structure of language better than starting from more complex sentences like Wikipedia or Proust.

items.question: How do you interpret the finding that giving a language model more complex training sentences helps it learn syntax?
items.object: Training language models on grammatically complex sentences
items.answer: I think you're pointing out a tension there that we should resolve. I'm not sure. What we said in that paper is that when you give the model a lot of complex sentences in training, it ends up learning more about syntax. Thinking on my feet right now—I hadn't thought about this before—I think what happened in that early experiment is that when we gave the model a lot of examples, we gave it a lot of counterexamples to the trick where you just look at the most recent word and decide based on that if the verb should be singular or plural. Eventually it figures it out, or at least does better than if you don't give it a lot of counterexamples. Obviously, that's not so interesting, because what we really care about is models that learn from the normal distribution of sentences. You don't want to have to give the model counterexamples to the wrong rules it might learn; you just want it to learn the right rules from the natural distribution.

items.question: Why do you think child-directed speech might help a language model learn syntactic structure more effectively?
items.object: Child-directed speech as a source for learning syntactic structure
items.answer: My hypothesis for why child-directed speech might be more effective in bootstrapping syntactic structure is that it has a lot of short, simple sentences and even fragments. Sometimes the whole thing the child hears is just a noun phrase, like “the red balloon.” That tells you, “Okay, ‘the red balloon’ is its own thing; let me think of it as a constituent if I ever see it again in other sentences.” Those simple units bootstrap your grammar induction. If all the sentences you see are incredibly long—the average sentence in Wikipedia is, I think, 20 words long—you don't know where to start. You need a lot more examples to find commonalities between sentences and figure out that this sequence of words is the subject in both of them. I'm really speculating here. We have a couple of projects trying to explore the different hypotheses in this space, but I don't have anything empirical to say about it yet.

items.question: How do you view the idea of teaching language models syntax through a curriculum that progresses from simple sentences to more complex structures?
items.object: A curriculum for teaching language models syntax that progresses from simple sentences to complex structures
items.answer: Yeah, absolutely. I agree that that's how humans also learn language. They don't start by listening to audiobooks. They start with these very simple sentences, and then at the age of, whatever, six, they start reading longer and longer sentences and more complex structures.
quotes: Yeah, absolutely.

items.question: How do you understand the hypothesis that Transformers represent syntactic trees across their layers?
items.object: The hypothesis that Transformers represent syntactic trees across their layers
items.answer: In that discussion, we were inspired by work from Shikhar Murty. I think he would be the person to ask about this hypothesis and how he tests it. Basically, the hypothesis is that the tree is literally represented across the layers of the Transformer. If a span is a constituent, you would see this little column across the Transformer that represents that span. If the depth of the tree is, let's say, 13, you might literally need 13 layers to represent that entire sentence in that way. If you have fewer than 13 layers, you're going to have to start approximating it and your behavior will be worse. That's the hypothesis: you build bigger and bigger constituents as you go deeper in the network, and shallower networks have to find different ways of accomplishing the same thing that are less reliable and generalize less well.

That's the hypothesis: you build bigger and bigger constituents as you go deeper in the network, and shallower networks have to find different ways of accomplishing the same thing that are less reliable and generalize less well.

items.question: Why do you think language models need stronger inductive biases to learn from the amount of data available to humans?
items.object: Inductive biases for learning language from human-scale amounts of data
items.answer: I think we do need stronger inductive biases than we have now to learn language from the amount of data that people learn from. One of our other recent papers looked at learning to form questions. We looked at child-directed speech and all the questions we have in the English part of the child speech corpus, and trained the neural network to form a question from the declarative sentence that it's equivalent to. The model was not able to learn to do that from the amount of evidence in child-directed speech. If you give it a lot more evidence, it will eventually be able to do that, but it does seem that humans are more efficient in that way. That efficiency can come from a lot of sources. One source could be architectural inductive biases, like having a tendency to construct trees for sentences and then perform all the tasks you want to do with the sentence on that tree rather than on the sequence of words. That's one way to bias a model to learn more efficiently. I don't know if it's the only way. We're exploring different options there.

The model was not able to learn to do that from the amount of evidence in child-directed speech. If you give it a lot more evidence, it will eventually be able to do that, but it does seem that humans are more efficient in that way. That efficiency can come from a lot of sources. One source could be architectural inductive biases, like having a tendency to construct trees for sentences and then perform all the tasks you want to do with the sentence on that tree rather than on the sequence of words. That's one way to bias a model to learn more efficiently. I don't know if it's the only way. We're exploring different options there.

rubrics.text: The response states that a neural network failed to learn to transform declarative sentences into corresponding English questions from the amount of evidence available in child-directed speech.
The response states that the neural network can eventually learn question formation when given substantially more training evidence.
The response identifies operating on sentence trees rather than word sequences as a possible architectural inductive bias for learning language more efficiently from limited data.

items.question: How do you think a model’s purpose should determine whether it reproduces human errors in logical reasoning?
items.object: Reproducing human logical reasoning errors in AI models
items.answer: I think it's important to keep in mind what you're trying to accomplish with a certain model. One example at the top of my mind right now is logical reasoning. We have a project on logical reasoning, and humans are famously not very good at it. By logical reasoning I mean things like, “Some actors are bakers. Some bakers are chemists. Does it entail that some artists are chemists?” That kind of classic syllogistic reasoning goes back to Aristotle or something. People are really bad at this. That makes you wonder: would you ever want a language model that makes the same logical reasoning errors that humans make? Probably not. It's not clear what the purpose of that would be, other than passing the Turing test, which is kind of a dumb goal. But if you really want to pass the Turing test, you probably want to make the same errors humans make. For practical applications, it's not desirable for an AI system to have the same issues humans have in reasoning. But if the goal is to understand how humans reason and you want to use models for that, maybe you would construct two different models implementing two different hypotheses about how humans reason. If one makes errors more similar to human errors than the other, that simulation provides some support for the first theory about how humans reason. Then mimicking human errors becomes a good thing, but it really depends on your goals.
